question: A 68-year-old man with known atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, complete, painless loss of vision in his right eye that occurred 2 hours ago. Fundoscopy reveals a milky-white oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea, and markedly attenuated arterioles. The veins appear normal in calibre. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CRVO produces the 'blood-and-thunder' fundus with massively dilated and tortuous veins, flame haemorrhages in all quadrants, disc swelling, and cotton wool spots. The veins here are normal, ruling out CRVO.

Correct. CRAO produces: (1) milky-white retinal oedema (ischaemic swelling of inner retinal layers), (2) cherry-red spot at the fovea (choroidal circulation still visible through the thin foveal retina), (3) markedly attenuated arterioles, and (4) normal veins. AF is a risk factor for embolic CRAO.

Incorrect. BRAO causes a segmental, wedge-shaped area of retinal whitening corresponding to the territory of the occluded branch artery. Complete visual loss with diffuse retinal whitening and a cherry-red spot indicates central (not branch) arterial occlusion.

Incorrect. AION produces disc swelling (pale or hyperaemic), an altitudinal visual field defect (not complete loss), and no cherry-red spot. The retina itself appears normal in AION as the occlusion is at the level of the optic nerve head.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key: CRAO = cherry-red spot, white retina, thin arterioles, normal veins. CRVO = blood-and-thunder (haemorrhages everywhere, dilated tortuous veins, disc swelling). Mechanism: CRAO = embolic/thrombotic arterial; CRVO = venous thrombosis.

Perfect. Cherry-red spot + milky retina + attenuated arterioles + normal veins = CRAO. The cherry-red spot occurs because the fovea has no overlying ganglion cell layer and shows the red choroid through the thinned retina.
